reason: The chamber has a marked wall slot, and heart muscle provides the pumping force.

reason: The valves' reverse-flow picture matches the chambers' direction-control slot.

reason: Hemoglobin has oxygen-binding sites and should fit inside the red-cell envelopes.

reaction: The contrast with the muscle cells is interesting.
reason: Red blood cells should be carried in plasma to form blood.
expectation: Combining them will make blood that can carry oxygen through the vessels.

effect: The red blood cells and plasma formed oxygen-carrying blood; the vessels still need an exchange route.
reaction: The picture makes it clear that hemoglobin is inside the cells while sugar is dissolved in plasma.
reason: Capillary networks can connect the arteries and veins while providing thin walls for exchange.
expectation: The capillaries will connect the vessels into a route for exchange and return to the heart.

effect: The capillaries connected the arteries and veins into a vessel circuit with thin walls beside tissue cells.
reaction: The outward and return arrows make the route clear.
reason: The circuit needs blood to carry oxygen and dissolved sugar to tissues.
expectation: The blood will fill the circuit so it can deliver supplies through the capillaries.

alternatives.reason: The circuit also needs to connect to the pump.

effect: The blood-filled circuit completes the exchange route, and the new goal is to circulate the blood.
reaction: The inset clarifies that materials cross the capillary wall while red cells stay inside.
reason: The beating heart can pump blood through the filled circuit.
expectation: The heart will connect to the circuit and circulate the blood.

effect: The heart and blood-filled circuit formed a closed circulation, completing the chapter’s goals.
reaction: The return arrows make the repeated circuit clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making red blood cells was most worthwhile because their lack of mitochondria and their use of sugar for ATP contrasted with the muscle cells built earlier.

leastWorthwhile.text: Adding blood to the vessel circuit was straightforward and offered less to work out, though the exchange inset clarified what crosses the capillary wall.

surprise.text: I was surprised that the red blood cells still make ATP from sugar despite having no nucleus or mitochondria.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary; the item names and picture descriptions gave each combination a clear purpose.

continue.text: I would choose to continue to see how circulation connects with the other systems. The red-cell contrast and tissue-exchange picture made those relationships interesting.
